title: The little horn and the king of fierce face (Dan 8:9–12, 23–25)
speaker: Gabriel
description: From one of the four kingdoms a fierce, cunning king arises who destroys the holy people, removes the continual offering, opposes the prince of princes, and is broken without human hand.
in_text_interpretation: The little horn is a king arising "in the latter time of their kingdom" (8:23) — i.e. of the four kingdoms of Greece. He is not named.

interpretations.label: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
proponents: Josephus (Ant. 12.7.6: the desolation "according to the prophecy of Daniel")
S. R. Driver (1900): "admitted on all hands"
interpretations.summary: Textual reasoning: the horn comes from one of the four Greek kingdoms; it removes the continual offering and desolates the sanctuary, which 1 Maccabees records under Antiochus (1:54) until the rededication (4:52). Objection (Newton): a horn signifies a kingdom, not one man, and Antiochus's kingdom was not "exceedingly great". Acceptance: Driver says it is "admitted on all hands"; even Jerome, who resists Antiochus for ch. 7, accepts him here.

referents.symbol: Little horn / king of fierce face

interpretations.label: Antiochus as a type of the future Antichrist (dual fulfillment)
interpretations.summary: Because the vision concerns "the time of the end" (8:17, 19), the near fulfillment in Antiochus prefigures a final Antichrist. The future part is not a claim of historical fulfillment; the Antiochus part is recorded separately.

referents.referent: Antiochus as type; the Antichrist as antitype

interpretations.label: Rome (historicist)
interpretations.summary: The little horn of the goat is a new kingdom that arose out of one of the four — Rome, which conquered Macedonia and the East and later continued as the Greek empire. Newton rejects Antiochus "not very judiciously" identified. Objection (Driver): the horn grows "out of one of them", i.e. from a Greek kingdom, and its deeds match Antiochus's.
